title: UOps, rewrites, bounds
why: Everything later in the course is a rewrite on one hash-consed graph of (op, src, arg) nodes, so this module sets the data structure you will live in for 14 modules. Getting interning, cached properties and interval bounds right now prevents compounding slop later.

steps.title: Handout page 1: the format and grammar
steps.detail: Read page 1 only: tokens (DEF, REF, INT, BOOL, OP, ATTR, brackets), the 4-line grammar, filename prefixes and immediate limits. Write the grammar on paper before coding.

steps.title: Tokenizer and parser
steps.detail: Turn a .uir file into a list of bindings (name, op, atoms, attrs); handle comments, hex, leading zeros, %x= vs %x =, and [ ] sugar. Make comments_and_spacing, xor_hex, leading_zeros, stack_sugar_same parse; REJECT rejected_undefined_ref, rejected_redefined, rejected_unknown_op, rejected_int_literal_range.

steps.title: tinygrad-notes: UOp is a singleton
steps.detail: How a metaclass cache makes structural equality equal object identity; then glance at UOpMetaClass in ops.py (https://github.com/tinygrad/tinygrad/blob/b91fe2773cbc1a33c38c90b55c835e26be42a335/tinygrad/uop/ops.py#L181).

steps.title: Interned UOp(op, src, arg)
steps.detail: Build nodes through one constructor keyed by (op, src, arg) so equal triples return the same object. Pass hashcons_same_node.uir and make the node/edge counter that overbudget_many_nodes needs.

steps.title: Lazy dtype and shape + validator
steps.detail: Cache dtype/shape per node; reject dtype mismatches, ALU on vectors, free params, missing args, unreachable nodes, missing/used assert. Targets: all rejected_* except the index/limits ones (add_dtype_mismatch, alu_on_vector, stack_mixed, where_cond_int, div_bool, free_param, no_assert, assert_used, unreachable, vector_return, two_params_one_slot, missing_arg, arg_dtype).

steps.title: Handout page 2: the operation reference table
steps.detail: Read the Bounds and Cost columns row by row: wrapping widens to I, div/mod endpoint rules, xor exact-only-for-singletons, shl hull, cmplt/where.

steps.title: tinygrad UOp._min_max (vmin/vmax)
steps.detail: Read _min_max after drafting your own: note how each op derives bounds from source bounds, then skim test/null/test_uop_vmin_vmax.py (https://github.com/tinygrad/tinygrad/blob/b91fe2773cbc1a33c38c90b55c835e26be42a335/test/null/test_uop_vmin_vmax.py).

steps.title: Bounds and index/limit safety
steps.detail: Implement interval bounds per the table and use them to prove index and call-argument safety across all calls. Pass index_param_safe, index_mod_bounds_safe, index_stack and rejected_index_oob, rejected_index_const_oob, rejected_index_unbounded, rejected_arg_outside_limits, rejected_limits_reversed.

steps.title: Cost and budgets
steps.detail: Cost per node once (call = 1 + C(body) each time), then the three budget checks in the right order (bytes before parse, nodes/edges after parse, cost after validation). Pass overbudget_file_size, overbudget_many_nodes, overbudget_static_cost, cost_under_budget.

steps.title: Evaluator
steps.detail: Interpret the graph with exact i32 wrap, floor div/mod with the divide-by-zero conventions, shl mod 32, bool add/mul semantics, and call/param substitution. Pass every MATCH and mismatch_* file: run python3 run_tests.py 1.

steps.title: tinygrad-notes: pattern matcher, then UPat/PatternMatcher source
steps.detail: Read the note, then UPat (https://github.com/tinygrad/tinygrad/blob/b91fe2773cbc1a33c38c90b55c835e26be42a335/tinygrad/uop/ops.py#L1429), PatternMatcher (https://github.com/tinygrad/tinygrad/blob/b91fe2773cbc1a33c38c90b55c835e26be42a335/tinygrad/uop/ops.py#L1572) and graph_rewrite (https://github.com/tinygrad/tinygrad/blob/b91fe2773cbc1a33c38c90b55c835e26be42a335/tinygrad/uop/ops.py#L1877).

steps.title: UPat + PatternMatcher + graph_rewrite to fixed point
steps.detail: Write a matcher over (op, src patterns, named captures) and a bottom-up rewrite loop that reaches a fixed point; check yourself against test/null/test_pattern_matcher.py (https://github.com/tinygrad/tinygrad/blob/b91fe2773cbc1a33c38c90b55c835e26be42a335/test/null/test_pattern_matcher.py).

steps.title: Constant folding and identities
steps.detail: Rules: fold all-constant ALU via your evaluator, x+0, x*1, x*0, x^x, max(x,x), where(true,a,b). Verify every MATCH test folds to assert c c; compare to symbolic_simple in https://github.com/tinygrad/tinygrad/blob/b91fe2773cbc1a33c38c90b55c835e26be42a335/tinygrad/uop/symbolic.py#L123.

steps.title: Write 10 tests of your own
steps.detail: Target obvious-but-wrong compilers: wrap at INT_MIN, div/mod by negative, index bounds that only fail on the second call, shared vs distinct cost. Check each with the oracle (only after passing 65/65).

check: python3 run_tests.py 1 passes 65/65

Every MATCH test rewrites to assert c c through your PatternMatcher

outcomes: After this module you can represent a program as a typed UOp DAG and validate it against a spec.
After this module you can write pattern-matching rewrite rules and run them to a fixed point.
After this module you can compute integer value bounds (vmin/vmax) through ALU ops and use them to fold code.
After this module you can explain why a rewrite is sound and when it is not (overflow, division semantics).
stuck: Rewrites that never terminate: usually two rules undo each other (a+b -> b+a). Canonicalize operand order instead of swapping.
Bounds wrong for division/modulo with negatives: C truncates toward zero, Python floors. Pick one semantics and test negative operands explicitly.
Constant folding changed results: you folded in Python ints but the target is int32. Wrap to the dtype width when folding.
Validator passes but evaluator crashes: check every src arity/dtype in the validator, not only the op name.
Rewrites applied to a node but children unchanged: rewrite bottom-up and rebuild parents when any child changes (hash-cons nodes).

project.title: Proved-correct symbolic simplifier with a rewrite visualizer
project.brief: Turn your rewrite engine into a verified simplifier: encode every integer rewrite rule as a z3 query over bitvectors (int32 wraparound included) and refuse to load rules that are not proven equivalent under their stated preconditions. Add a tracer that records each rule firing and renders before/after DAGs per pass, so you can show exactly how an index expression collapses.
deliverables: repo with a rule file, a z3 checker CLI (check_rules) and CI that fails on any unproven rule
an HTML or Graphviz trace viewer showing each rewrite step on 3+ real index expressions from later modules

a 600–1200 word write-up on one rule z3 rejected, why it was wrong, and the corrected precondition

rubric.exceptional: Finds and documents at least one real unsound rule (yours or in a published compiler) with a counterexample; uses bounds as z3 assumptions so conditional rules are proven too; compares against an egg-style e-graph on the same set.

title: Loads, stores, memory; render C
why: Memory introduces effects, so graph order is no longer free: a load must be ordered after the stores it observes. This module is also your first real backend: toposort, emit C, compile with clang, call through ctypes.

steps.title: 10-411 syllabus: Week 2
steps.detail: Read the Week 2 section (BUFFER/LOAD/STORE/AFTER, 'loads and stores must be fully ordered') and the README Week 2 spec side by side.

steps.title: Parse nested (op ...) expressions and new ops
steps.detail: Extend the parser for extern, store, load, after, index-on-buffer, and nested parenthesised operands anywhere an atom goes. Week 1 tests must still pass.

steps.title: Russ Cox, Hardware Memory Models: sections 'Sequential Consistency' and 'x86-TSO'
steps.detail: Only these two sections; the point is why compilers/hardware reorder unordered memory ops, motivating AFTER.

steps.title: Preshing, Memory Ordering at Compile Time
steps.detail: Short: how a compiler reorders loads/stores and what a compiler barrier is.

steps.title: Ordering validator
steps.detail: Track, per buffer, the stores reachable through after; REJECT unordered loads and out-of-range or dtype-wrong stores (reuse Week 1 bounds). Pass rejected_load_without_after, rejected_store_oob, rejected_store_dtype.

steps.title: Interpreter support for memory
steps.detail: Extend the Week 1 evaluator with buffers so it executes store/load/after in dependency order. Pass store_load, index_store, two_stores_ordered, read_modify_write, mismatch_stale_read.

steps.title: tinygrad linearize (toposort to a list)
steps.detail: Read linearize() and UOp.toposort (https://github.com/tinygrad/tinygrad/blob/b91fe2773cbc1a33c38c90b55c835e26be42a335/tinygrad/uop/ops.py#L281) to see how a graph becomes a straight-line program.

steps.title: Toposort + C emitter
steps.detail: Emit one loopless C function: one local per node in topo order, buffers as pointer args, int32_t with wrapping semantics (cast through uint32_t to avoid UB).

steps.title: tinygrad renderer/cstyle.py: base_rewrite and ClangRenderer
steps.detail: Read base_rewrite (lines 9-82) and ClangRenderer (line 283): rendering is just another PatternMatcher from UOp to string.

steps.title: Python ctypes: loading shared libraries and arrays
steps.detail: Sections 'Loading dynamic link libraries', 'Arrays' and 'Specifying the required argument types'. (Or dlopen if not Python.)

steps.detail: Write .c to a temp dir, compile, dlopen, allocate buffers, call, compare to assert. All week01 and week02 tests through the C backend.

steps.title: Cross-check the two backends
steps.detail: Run interpreter and C on every test and diff results; add 10 tests (e.g. two stores to the same index, store whose index is only safe via mod bounds, signed overflow that clang would treat as UB).

build: A C backend: toposort, render one loopless function, compile with clang, run via ctypes, with the interpreter as a cross-check.
check: python3 run_tests.py 2 and 1 pass through the C backend
Unordered loads and out-of-range stores are REJECTED

outcomes: After this module you can topologically order a UOp graph and emit straight-line C from it.
After this module you can compile generated C at runtime with clang and call it through ctypes with NumPy buffers.
After this module you can use an interpreter as a reference to cross-check a code generator.

stuck: Segfaults from ctypes: argument types not declared (argtypes) or a non-contiguous NumPy array. Use np.ascontiguousarray and set argtypes.
Results differ by tiny amounts: clang with -ffast-math reorders floats. Compare with a tolerance, or drop fast-math while debugging.
Same node rendered twice or used before defined: your toposort is not visiting shared children once. Memoize by node identity.
Stale .so loaded: dlopen caches by path. Name the library by a hash of the source.
Integer overflow silently UB in C: use explicit int32/uint32 casts that match your interpreter's semantics.

title: Loops, floats, runtime; matmul and conv

title: Rangeify, reduce, materialization
why: Rangeify lowers shaped ops into scalar code over explicit ranges and decides what to materialize; that is the scheduler at the heart of every ML compiler. Fusion vs staging is where performance is won or lost.

stuck: Fusing a reduce into its consumer recomputes the reduce per output element: materialize when a reduce result is used by more than one loop iteration.

outcomes: After this module you can write a 4-page technical report with clear claims backed by numbers.
After this module you can present your work in a 15-minute talk with a live or recorded demo.
After this module you can package code so a stranger reproduces your results.
After this module you can discuss limitations and threats to validity like a reviewer would.
stuck: Report lists what you did instead of what you found: lead with the claim and the headline number.
Plots without baselines or error bars: every chart needs a comparison and variance.
Talk too detailed: one idea, one key figure, one demo; backup slides for the rest.
Reproduction fails on a fresh machine: test the README on a clean container or cloud VM before publishing.

project.title: Capstone phase 3: public technical report, talk and demo
project.brief: Publish a 4-page report (arXiv-style PDF or blog post), a 15-minute recorded talk with a live demo of your compiler (training MNIST and generating text on your GPU plus the project result), and a reproducible artifact. Share it publicly and ask practitioners for feedback.
deliverables: public repo with one-command reproduction and a results table matching the report
4-page report: problem, method, results, ablations, negative results, limitations, related work
15-minute recorded talk with slides and demo, linked from the README
a short post (blog, X, HN, tinygrad/GPU MODE Discord) with the headline figure, and notes on feedback received

rubric.solid: Report is self-contained and every number reproduces; talk fits 15 minutes with a working demo.
rubric.exceptional: Report is good enough for a workshop submission (e.g. an MLSys/ASPLOS workshop) or gets substantive engagement from engineers at a compiler/kernel team; a stranger reproduces your results and confirms it.
